title: Topic 8 - Monetary Policy in Crisis and Recovery
text:
Question 1: UK Economic Shocks Since 2010 and Bank of England Responses





Discuss the four shocks to have hit the UK economy since 2010. How has the Bank of England responded to each of these shocks and how has this response compared with its initial response following the sub-prime market crash of July 2007?









Question 2: Post-Great Recession Modifications to Monetary Policy Consensus





How did the conduct of monetary policy by major central banks in the period after the Great Recession modify the monetary policy consensus that prevailed during the Great Moderation?

Question 2: Post-Great Recession Modifications to Monetary Policy Consensus

crumbs: Topic 8 - Monetary Policy in the Post-Crisis

title: Topic 8 - Indicative Answers
text:
Tip





The Four Shocks to the UK Economy


The eurozone faced a sovereign debt crisis starting with Greece, spreading to Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Italy. This created spillover effects to the UK through: - Trade linkages (reduced eurozone demand for UK exports) - Financial linkages (UK banks had exposure to eurozone debt) - Confidence effects (risk aversion reduced cross-border investment)
BoE Response: The BoE maintained historically low interest rates and expanded quantitative easing (QE) programs to support the UK economy while eurozone policy was constrained by fiscal austerity rules. The BoE provided expansionary support independently because eurozone central banks were pursuing tight policy.



The June 2016 Brexit referendum vote to leave the European Union created significant uncertainty: - Currency depreciation (pound fell ~10-15% post-vote) - Investment uncertainty (businesses delayed capital expenditure) - Consumer confidence shocks (expectations of job losses, inflation)
BoE Response: Initially, the BoE cut rates and restarted QE post-referendum to support growth. However, the BoE also faced an inflation problem from currency depreciation, creating a policy dilemma. The BoE provided expansionary policy while managing inflation expectations—again, largely acting alone as other central banks weren’t facing similar shocks.



The global pandemic induced the sharpest recession in modern times: - Lockdowns shut down large parts of the economy - Unemployment spiked sharply - Output fell ~20% in Q2 2020 - Financial markets experienced severe stress and illiquidity
BoE Response: This was unprecedented in scale and speed. The BoE: - Cut rates to near-zero (0.1%) almost immediately - Expanded QE programs dramatically (£200+ billion purchases) - Introduced lending facilities to support credit to businesses (CCFF, CBILS) - Coordinated with other major central banks (Fed, ECB) and governments
Key difference from 2007: Unlike the initial 2007 response (gradual rate cuts over time), the 2020 response was immediate, large-scale, and multi-dimensional. Importantly, this was coordinated with other major central banks and fiscal authorities, not a unilateral BoE response.



As COVID restrictions lifted: - Pent-up demand rebounded sharply - Supply chains remained disrupted - Energy prices surged dramatically (Russian invasion of Ukraine, OPEC+ production cuts) - Inflation rose from 1-2% to 10%+ (October 2022 peak)
BoE Response: Facing generational high inflation, the BoE: - Raised rates from near-zero to 5.25% by August 2023 (fastest pace in decades) - Ended QE and began quantitative tightening (selling assets) - Communicated aggressively about inflation-fighting credentials - Accepted that output would fall and unemployment would rise to bring inflation down

Comparison with 2007 Initial Response








Aspect
2007 Response
Post-2010 Response




Speed
Gradual rate cuts over time
Rapid, sometimes immediate


Scope
Traditional monetary policy (interest rates, eventually QE)
Multi-faceted: rates + QE + lending facilities + forward guidance


Coordination
Largely unilateral BoE action
Coordinated with other CBs and governments (especially 2020)


Real economy focus
Initially focused on financial stability, gradual real economy support
Explicitly directed at real economy support and employment (especially post-2010)


Communication
Less explicit about objectives and timelines
Highly transparent about objectives, timelines, and policy frameworks


Flexibility
Rigid adherence to inflation targeting initially
Context-dependent: inflation targets maintained but balanced against real economy needs



Key Insight: The BoE’s response evolved from a narrow focus on inflation stability (2007) toward a more holistic approach to economic stability, explicitly supporting real economy activity, and actively communicating its intentions. The BoE set aside the part of the Great Moderation consensus that suggested central banks should focus exclusively on inflation—while maintaining the emphasis on transparency and communication.














Tip





The Great Moderation Consensus
Before the Great Recession, there was a dominant monetary policy consensus built on two pillars:

Inflation Stability = Overall Economic Stability: Central banks’ primary focus should be maintaining low and stable inflation. The logic was that this would promote overall macroeconomic stability, financial stability, and sustainable growth.
The Policy Framework: The appropriate tool for achieving this is interest rate targeting (typically an inflation target of ~2%), using the policy rate as the main instrument, with the assumption that markets would function efficiently and transmission mechanisms would operate reliably.

This consensus reflected the belief that: - Central banks should have a single, narrow mandate (price stability) - Financial markets self-correct through rational expectations - There are no trade-offs between inflation stability and other macro objectives - Central banks should be independent but accountable for inflation performance
How Post-Great Recession Policy Challenged This


The Problem: Following the 2008 crash, the Fed, ECB, and BoE cut rates to near-zero. But the economy remained depressed—unemployment stayed high, growth remained sluggish, and inflation fell below target. Traditional monetary policy had “run out of ammunition.”
The Modification: Central banks adopted quantitative easing (QE)—direct purchases of long-term securities to inject liquidity and lower longer-term rates. This represented an admission that: - The policy interest rate alone may not be sufficient, especially at the zero lower bound - Central banks must be willing to use unconventional tools when conventional tools are exhausted - Central bank balance sheets and asset purchases matter for inflation and output
Implication: The narrow focus on the policy interest rate as the main lever was abandoned in favour of a broader toolkit that includes QE, forward guidance, negative rates (in some countries), and lending facilities.



The Problem: The 2008 crisis demonstrated that you can have price stability yet face a severe recession. Inflation was tame (~2%) before the crash, yet the financial system nearly collapsed and real output fell sharply.
The Modification: Central banks acknowledged that: - Financial stability must be a separate objective alongside price stability - Macro-prudential regulation (capital requirements, stress testing, countercyclical buffers) should complement monetary policy - Central banks must monitor financial imbalances, credit growth, and asset price bubbles—not just inflation - A single-minded focus on inflation targeting can miss risks to overall economic stability
Implication: Central banks began explicitly incorporating financial stability considerations into their policy frameworks, even when this meant accepting higher inflation temporarily to support financial stability or real activity.



The Problem: The Great Moderation consensus emphasized inflation targeting as a permanent, non-negotiable commitment. But different shocks and different circumstances may require different priorities: - During the eurozone crisis, unemployment was high; inflation was low. Focusing rigidly on inflation targets would have meant tighter policy, worsening unemployment - During COVID, the initial priority was financial stability and preventing economic collapse, not hitting inflation targets - During post-COVID inflation, unemployment was low; inflation was high. The balance shifted toward fighting inflation
The Modification: Central banks adopted a more flexible, pragmatic approach where: - The inflation target remains the long-run anchor, but the policy timeline is flexible - Real economy considerations (employment, growth) are balanced against inflation, not subordinated to it - Communication is explicit about trade-offs and priorities given the current shock - Forward guidance and transparency substitute for rigid rules
Implication: Modern central banking is more discretionary than the Great Moderation consensus suggested. The consensus view that “rules are better than discretion” gave way to “credible discretion with transparent communication.”



The Problem: The Great Moderation consensus implied narrow independence: central banks should focus on inflation, period. But post-crisis reality showed central banks had to act on multiple fronts (financial stability, employment, credit, real economy support).
The Modification: Central banks: - Expanded mandates explicitly (e.g., Fed’s dual mandate includes employment; ECB added financial stability) - Increased transparency about how they balance multiple objectives - Engaged in “forward guidance” to manage expectations - Acknowledged accountability not just for inflation but for overall macroeconomic outcomes - Coordinated with fiscal authorities, which was taboo under the Great Moderation consensus
Implication: Central banks became more accountable for real economy outcomes and less insulated from political pressures. The independence-accountability balance shifted.

Summary of Modifications








Dimension
Great Moderation Consensus
Post-Great Recession Reality




Primary Tool
Policy interest rate
Policy rate + QE + forward guidance + lending facilities


Objective
Price stability (narrow)
Price stability + financial stability + employment (broad)


Policy Philosophy
Rules-based, non-discretionary
Flexible, context-dependent with transparent communication


Mandate
Narrow (inflation only)
Expanded (inflation, employment, financial stability)


Coordination
Independent action
Coordination with other CBs and governments


Transparency
Important but secondary
Central to credibility and managing expectations



Key Insight: Post-Great Recession monetary policy abandoned the idea that central banks should have a single, narrow focus on inflation targeting. Instead, modern central banks pursue a more balanced approach toward overall economic stability, with explicit real economy objectives, broader policy tools, and stronger communication. Transparency and credibility remain valued, but they now serve the broader goal of macroeconomic and financial stability, not just inflation control.

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
By the early 1990s, a widely taught “monetary policy consensus” emerged in advanced economies: monetary policy should prioritize price stability, implemented by an independent central bank using a short‑term policy interest rate, with communication and accountability designed to anchor inflation expectations and reduce macroeconomic volatility. This view became closely associated with the “Great Moderation,” the period of reduced volatility in output growth and inflation in many advanced economies from the mid‑1980s until the global financial crisis (Bernanke, 2004).
In the UK, the political narrative of “stability” became highly salient. A famous statement often associated with this period is Gordon Brown’s “no return to boom and bust,” recorded in a 2006 Budget statement.
The consensus did not imply that recessions were impossible. Many emerging and developing economies continued to experience episodes of currency and financial crisis during the 1990s (for example, crises associated with fixed or heavily managed exchange rates). An IMF analysis by Stanley Fischer—reflecting on crises in Asia, Russia and elsewhere—explicitly highlighted the vulnerability of “more or less fixed” exchange-rate systems to crisis pressure.
This chapter is designed to replace the relevant student reading from Lewis & Mizen (2000), Chapter 16, while preserving and enhancing the core lecture-note ideas with modern academic and institutional sources.








Figure 1: Great Moderation and consensus-era timeline showing key milestones from 1990s inflation targeting adoption through COVID and recent tightening cycles













Figure 2: UK inflation volatility (rolling 5-year standard deviation) illustrating the Great Moderation period of reduced volatility







After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

Explain the core propositions of the monetary policy consensus (long‑run nominal anchor, short‑run real effects via frictions/surprises, credibility problems).
Compare three anti‑inflation strategies: monetary targeting, fixed exchange rates, and inflation targeting—and explain why inflation targeting became dominant.
Describe how the UK inflation‑targeting system works (objective setting, operational independence, transparency, and the open‑letter accountability mechanism).
Evaluate the choice of inflation target (including why “0%” is risky) and explain the difference between inflation targeting and price‑level targeting.

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
2.1 Long-run: monetary policy anchors inflation
A central pillar of the consensus is a long‑run monetarist proposition: persistent inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon, in the practical sense that a central bank that sets the nominal anchor can, over time, determine the long‑run inflation rate.
Modern central banks state this in policy‑framework documents. For example, the Federal Reserve’s strategy statement explicitly notes that “the inflation rate over the longer run is primarily determined by monetary policy,” and therefore the committee can specify a longer‑run inflation goal (Federal Reserve, 2025).
For undergraduates, you can interpret this as: in the long run, monetary policy cannot permanently raise real GDP growth, but it can deliver low and stable inflation, which improves decision-making and long-horizon planning.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 2.2 Short-run: monetary policy can affect real activity, but only under specific conditions
text:
2.2 Short-run: monetary policy can affect real activity, but only under specific conditions
The consensus emphasizes two situations where money can affect real variables in the short run:

Unexpected policy innovations (surprises). In the rational expectations tradition, real effects come from the unexpected component of policy—not the predictable component. Robert Lucas’s classic analysis derives a Phillips‑curve‑like relation while excluding “money illusion,” implying that systematic, anticipated policy does not reliably buy higher output; only surprise elements can.
Nominal rigidities. Even without deliberate deception, if wages and prices adjust slowly, changes in interest rates can influence real spending and production before prices fully adjust. Modern central bank explanations of transmission explicitly highlight nominal rigidities as a reason policy affects real activity.

The consensus interpretation is careful: short‑run real effects are temporary, while the lasting effect of sustained monetary expansion is on nominal variables (especially the price level). In lecture terms: “real effects wear off; nominal effects persist.”
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 2.3 A built-in tension: short-run stabilization versus long-run credibility
text:
2.3 A built-in tension: short-run stabilization versus long-run credibility
The consensus stresses that these short‑run effects create a conflict:

Short run: policymakers may be tempted to create a boom via surprise inflation (e.g., before an election).
Long run: the optimal role of monetary policy is to deliver low and predictable inflation.

Time inconsistency theory formalizes this temptation: discretionary “fine tuning” in pursuit of short‑run output gains can damage credibility, raising expected inflation and leading to worse outcomes.
This is why the consensus places special weight on reputation and credibility. A central bank known to be “soft” on inflation may find disinflation costly because private agents doubt the commitment; expectations adjust slowly and output losses can be larger. This logic is consistent with standard credibility models and with central banks’ ongoing emphasis on anchoring long‑term expectations.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 3.1 Price stability as the central bank’s primary macroeconomic contribution
text:
3.1 Price stability as the central bank’s primary macroeconomic contribution
The consensus view is that monetary policy’s comparative advantage is maintaining a stable nominal environment. Modern policy frameworks make this explicit. The ECB strategy statement says price stability is best maintained by aiming for 2% inflation over the medium term, and emphasizes the importance of the inflation target as an anchor for expectations.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
3.2 Independence from day-to-day politics
A central bank insulated from short-term political pressures is less likely to exploit short-run inflation-output trade-offs, and more likely to maintain credibility. In the UK, operational independence was introduced in 1997: the central bank was granted responsibility for setting the short-term policy interest rate to achieve an inflation target set by government (i.e., instrument independence).
The distinction remains crucial:

Operational (instrument) independence: the central bank chooses how to achieve the target.
Goal independence: the central bank also chooses the target (rare in practice).

UK policy continues to operate under operational independence: the inflation target is set by government and reaffirmed in remits, while the central bank chooses instruments to achieve it.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
3.3 Conservative central bank leadership
The consensus states that monetary conservatives should run central banks. In academic monetary theory, this idea is formalized as “conservative delegation”: appointing a central banker who places relatively high weight on inflation stabilization can reduce inflation bias, though it may raise stabilization costs under some shocks.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 3.4 Transparency and accountability when deviating from a low-inflation strategy
text:
3.4 Transparency and accountability when deviating from a low-inflation strategy
The consensus approach is not “no flexibility”; it is disciplined flexibility. When policy deviates from the target path, policymakers should explain why and how inflation will return to target. Modern inflation targeting frameworks embed this in:

Regular forecasts and reports
Published minutes and votes
Explicit accountability triggers

The UK open-letter mechanism is a concrete example: if inflation deviates from target by more than 1 percentage point (above 3% or below 1% on a 2% target), the Governor must write publicly to the Chancellor explaining the deviation and the strategy to return inflation to target.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
4.1 Monetary targeting
Monetary targeting uses a target path for a money aggregate (e.g., M1, M2, broad money) as an intermediate target to achieve low inflation.

4.1.1 The simple theoretical case
Start from a quantity-theory identity: \(MV = PY\). In growth rates, a convenient approximation is: \[\pi \approx \mu + \nu - g,\] where \(\pi\) is inflation, \(\mu\) is money growth, \(\nu\) is velocity growth, and \(g\) is real output growth. If velocity growth is stable (or near zero), targeting money growth consistent with output growth and desired inflation should, “on average,” stabilize inflation.
This is closely aligned with monetarist proposals for steady money growth (for example, a fixed \(k\)‑percent rule) and with the idea that predictability in monetary conditions can anchor expectations.


4.1.2 Why it broke down in practice
Two practical problems emerged:

Definitional and controllability problems. It is difficult to choose which monetary aggregate matters most, and central banks have tighter control over narrow aggregates than over broad aggregates created inside the banking system.
Instability of money demand (velocity instability). Even if the central bank can influence money growth, the relation between broad money and nominal income can become unreliable due to financial innovation and portfolio shifts.

A classic Bank of England analysis from the 1980s explicitly discussed how the relationship between broad money growth and nominal incomes became increasingly unpredictable in the UK after 1980, with velocity behavior changing substantially, raising the question of whether broad money targets should be abandoned.
This diagnosis appears in later central bank research as well: when the money–inflation relationship is unstable, hitting a money target may not reliably deliver the inflation outcome, weakening accountability and the anchor.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
4.2 Fixing the exchange rate
A fixed (or tightly managed) exchange rate can serve as a nominal anchor by “importing” the credibility of a low‑inflation anchor country.

4.2.1 The simple link between exchange rates and inflation
A stylized purchasing power parity relation suggests: \[\Delta e \approx \pi - \pi^*,\] where \(e\) is the nominal exchange rate (domestic currency per unit of foreign currency), and \(\pi^*\) is foreign inflation. If the exchange rate is fixed (\(\Delta e = 0\)), then domestic inflation tends to converge toward foreign inflation (\(\pi \approx \pi^*\)) in the long run.
This is an intuition, not a law: PPP is imprecise in the short run. But the key policy lesson is about constraints: a credible commitment to a peg can severely limit domestic monetary discretion.


4.2.2 Advantages (when credible)
Central bank research highlights two major benefits:

A clear, observable anchor that can reduce inflation expectations quickly.
A rule-like constraint that can mitigate the time inconsistency problem by putting monetary policy on “automatic pilot.”



4.2.3 Disadvantages and fragility (when credibility is imperfect)
The main costs include:

Loss of domestic policy autonomy. If the anchor country’s interest rate is inappropriate for domestic conditions, the pegging country cannot respond.
Balance of payments stress and reserve loss. Defending an overvalued peg depletes reserves; defending an undervalued peg can force persistent reserve accumulation and balance-sheet expansion.
Speculative attack risk. If markets believe a peg is inconsistent with fundamentals, rational speculation can become self-fulfilling: agents buy foreign currency before devaluation, accelerating reserve loss and precipitating collapse.

The UK’s 1992 ERM episode illustrates the internal-objective vs exchange-rate-commitment conflict: the Bank of England’s analysis describes how ERM membership constrained UK interest rate policy relative to Germany, raising real interest rates as domestic inflation pressures fell, and culminating in suspension of sterling’s ERM membership after heavy intervention.
A second canonical example is Argentina’s collapse of the convertibility regime. The IMF Independent Evaluation Office report describes how convertibility became “virtually impossible” to salvage amid collapsing confidence, leading to default and abandonment of the peg.
A contrasting case is a “harder” rules-based currency board. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority continues to defend its linked exchange rate system, emphasizing its transparency, rules-based nature, and large reserves as elements supporting credibility.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
4.3 Inflation targeting
Inflation targeting became the dominant consensus strategy in many economies because it combines:

A clear nominal anchor (the inflation target)
Domestic policy autonomy (unlike a peg)
Robustness to money-demand/velocity shocks (unlike strict monetary targeting)
Institutional reforms (communication and accountability) to cope with time inconsistency


4.3.1 What inflation targeting is
A widely used definition is that a central bank publicly announces a numerical inflation objective (often with a tolerance band) and commits institutionally to achieve it over a medium-term horizon, using all available information.
In the academic literature, Ben Bernanke and Frederic Mishkin argued that inflation targeting is best understood as “constrained discretion”: not a mechanical rule, but a framework that disciplines decisions through transparency, forecasts, and accountability.
In practice, most regimes are flexible inflation-targeting regimes: they aim to stabilize inflation around target while also smoothing output and employment fluctuations.


4.3.2 Why a tolerance band exists
A central bank does not control inflation directly; it affects inflation with lags through aggregate demand, expectations, and exchange rates. For credibility, regimes typically define a band (or operate with an implicit tolerance) so that small forecast errors or supply shocks do not automatically appear as “policy failure.”


4.3.3 The policy instrument: the short-term interest rate
Inflation targeting is implemented primarily through a short‑term policy rate (with money aggregates adjusting endogenously).
The Bank of England’s transmission-mechanism paper describes how the MPC sets the official short-term rate, which influences market rates, expectations, asset prices and the exchange rate, and then spending decisions, ultimately affecting inflation. More recent BoE work—explicitly linking nominal rigidities and expectations to transmission—reinforces the same core mechanism. The ECB’s transmission overview similarly highlights expectations, asset prices, exchange rates, and spending decisions as key channels.








Figure 4: Monetary transmission mechanism schematic showing how policy rates affect inflation through multiple channels







4.3.4 Inflation targeting after the Global Financial Crisis: the toolkit expands
The global financial crisis did not remove inflation targeting from the consensus; it expanded the toolkit when interest rates hit the effective lower bound. Concrete institutional examples:

The Bank of England explains that QE was introduced in March 2009 when Bank Rate was very low; QE lowers longer-term yields by purchasing bonds, supporting spending and helping meet the inflation target.
The Federal Reserve documents large-scale asset purchases beginning in 2008–09 (LSAP1), illustrating how balance-sheet tools were used when conventional rate cuts were constrained.
The Bank of Japan’s official reference timeline lists ZIRP (1999), QE (2001), QQE (2013), and later negative rates and yield curve control—illustrating sustained reliance on unconventional tools in a low-inflation environment.









Figure 5: Cross-country policy rates (BoE, ECB, Fed) with key event markers for crisis periods and unconventional policy adoptions













Figure 6: Quantitative easing envelope announcements showing stepped increases in BoE APF, ECB PEPP, and Fed LSAP1 programs

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 5.1 The UK framework: operational independence with a government-set target
text:
5.1 The UK framework: operational independence with a government-set target
The UK has operated modern inflation targeting since the early 1990s, with a major institutional change in 1997: operational independence for setting the policy rate to achieve the target. The Bank of England’s retrospective discussion of independence describes the 1997 arrangement and the construction of the MPC (monthly meetings, voting, published minutes).
Today, the inflation target is set by government, reaffirmed in the remit, and measured by CPI inflation. The 2025 remit letter explicitly reconfirms the 2% CPI target and the primacy of price stability, and describes the Bank’s statutory objectives (price stability, and subject to that, supporting government economic policy).
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
5.2 Accountability: open letters
If inflation deviates beyond the tolerance threshold, the Bank must provide an explanation in writing.
This mechanism is described clearly in HM Treasury’s “open letters” collection and the BoE’s public explanation of the 2% target: if CPI inflation is above 3% or below 1%, the Governor writes an open letter to the Chancellor explaining why inflation moved away from target and how policy will return it to target.








Figure 7: UK CPI inflation with 2% target and 1-3% open-letter threshold band since 1997 operational independence













Figure 8: UK Bank Rate (official policy instrument) evolution demonstrating operational independence era
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
5.3 Transparency: reports and forecasts
The Bank publishes regular Monetary Policy Reports as a major communication tool (renamed from “Inflation Report” in 2019 as part of changes designed to improve communication and accountability).
This evolution is consistent with the consensus idea that credibility is supported by regular, structured communication of:

current conditions,
forecasts (conditional on a policy path),
and the reaction function guiding decisions.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
5.4 Flexible inflation targeting in practice
The Bank does not aim to hit the target every month; it aims to return inflation to target over a horizon, justifying temporary deviations.
This “flexible” interpretation is also embedded in broader inflation targeting practice: supply shocks and trade-offs are handled by allowing inflation to return to target over a medium-term horizon, rather than forcing immediate reversal that would generate unnecessary output volatility.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
text:
5.5 Forward guidance: the UK 2013 example
Since the crisis, communication expanded to include forward guidance.
The August 2013 MPC minutes provide an official statement of the UK’s first explicit threshold-based forward guidance under Mark Carney: the MPC intended not to raise Bank Rate from 0.5% at least until the unemployment rate fell to 7%, subject to explicit “knockout” conditions related to the inflation outlook, inflation expectations anchoring, and financial stability.
This example illustrates two key consensus ideas simultaneously:

Expectations are part of the transmission mechanism.
Credibility requires conditional commitments that are clearly explained and constrained.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 6.1 Friedman’s optimal quantity of money and the Friedman rule
text:
6.1 Friedman’s optimal quantity of money and the Friedman rule
A standard presentation of the Friedman rule distinguishes between:

the k-percent money growth rule (a policy rule for money growth), and
the optimal quantity of money argument (a normative argument about the optimal nominal interest rate).

Because the marginal resource cost of producing base money is close to zero, the socially optimal policy makes it costless at the margin to hold money—implying a nominal interest rate near zero (\(i \approx 0\)). Using the Fisher relation \(i \approx r + \pi^e\), achieving \(i=0\) in steady state implies \(\pi \approx -r\) (a steady deflation roughly equal to the real interest rate).
This is a powerful theoretical benchmark—but it is not a practical policy recommendation in modern regimes.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 6.2 Why target inflation above zero: deflation risk, policy space, and wage adjustment
text:
6.2 Why target inflation above zero: deflation risk, policy space, and wage adjustment
Three reasons support inflation targeting above zero:

Deflation and debt burdens. Low or negative inflation can raise real debt burdens and amplify recessions through financial stress. Bernanke’s analysis highlights how deflation can create serious problems at the zero bound and references the debt‑deflation logic associated with Irving Fisher.
Policy space at the effective lower bound. If inflation is too low, then nominal interest rates are lower on average, leaving less room to cut rates in downturns. Once the nominal policy rate is at (or near) zero, conventional easing is constrained, complicating stabilization.
Modern frameworks explicitly acknowledge this constraint. For example, the FOMC’s 2020 statement notes that the long-run neutral rate has declined, increasing the frequency of effective‑lower‑bound episodes; it therefore adopted a strategy of aiming for inflation averaging 2% over time (seeking periods moderately above 2% following persistent undershoots) to help prevent expectations drifting downward.
Indirect real wage adjustment with nominal rigidities. With sticky nominal wages, positive inflation can facilitate real wage declines when needed, potentially speeding reallocation and recovery. Modern BoE analysis emphasizes nominal rigidities as central to why monetary policy transmits to real activity and inflation.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 6.3 Negative nominal rates: what happened in practice
text:
6.3 Negative nominal rates: what happened in practice
Some central bankers viewed negative nominal rates as infeasible, yet the ECB and others implemented them.
An ECB press release documents the introduction of a negative deposit facility rate (−0.10%) effective June 2014. A BIS survey article finds that modestly negative policy rates transmitted through money markets and other rates largely similarly to positive rates, though retail deposit rates were more insulated.
Together, these episodes refine the lecture point: negative rates are possible but operationally and politically constrained, strengthening the case for a small positive inflation target to reduce how often policy must rely on the most unconventional measures.
crumbs: Topic 7 - Monetary Policy Consensus and the Great Moderation

title: The Monetary Policy Consensus
section: 6.4 Target inflation rates or the price level
text:
6.4 Target inflation rates or the price level
The difference can be illustrated with a simple example:

If inflation is 3% one year and the objective is to keep average CPI growth at 2%, then next year inflation should be below 2% (e.g., around 1%) to bring the price level back toward the intended path.
Under standard inflation targeting, “bygones are bygones”: the central bank aims to return inflation to 2% going forward, allowing the price level to drift upward permanently after an overshoot.

This is the inflation‑target vs price‑level‑target contrast:

Price-level targeting: commits to a path for \(P_t\) (no “base drift”).
Inflation targeting: commits to a path for \(\pi_t\) (allowing base drift).

In the research literature, Svensson’s analysis compares these regimes and shows that, under certain conditions, price-level targeting can reduce long-run price uncertainty and may improve outcomes under discretion.
Modern frameworks have experimented with “makeup” features that partially mimic price-level targeting without committing fully to a price-level path—for example, the Fed’s “average inflation” language adopted in 2020.

title: Topic 7 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
How to use this quiz



This quiz is designed as a formative self-assessment tool, not as a test.
Its purpose is to help you: - check your understanding of the key concepts from Topic 7, - identify which types of thinking you find more difficult, and - guide your revision before the tutorial and future assessments.


Each question belongs to one of four categories:

Subject Knowledge (SK): definitions, concepts, and facts.

Analysis (AN): understanding relationships and economic mechanisms.

Problem Solving (PS): applying concepts to new situations.

Mathematical Thinking (MT): working with equations and quantitative relationships.

Your score will be broken down by category so you can see where you are strong and where you need more practice.




You may use your notes and the lecture materials.
Take your time — the goal is understanding, not speed.
Use the Hints if you get stuck.
You may refresh and retry the quiz as many times as you like.





A low score is not a problem — it tells you what to focus on.
If you score low in:

SK: revise definitions and core concepts.
AN: revisit the logic of the models and examples.
PS: practise applying concepts to new cases.
MT: practise the mathematical calculations and equations.





The leaderboard is optional and anonymous. It exists only to make practice more engaging.
It has no effect on your grade and is not used for evaluation.
The only purpose of this quiz is to support your learning.

title: Topic 6 - Central Bank Credibility and Inflation Control
text:
Question 1: Central Bank Loss Function and Inflation Bias





Explain why, if the public expect the central bank to set inflation at the equilibrium level \(\pi = \frac{bκλ}{a}\), the central bank will set this inflation rate, rather than \(\pi = 0\), even if it has no intention to create a “surprise” inflation.









Question 2: Fixed Exchange Rates and Inflation Credibility

Briefly discuss other methods by which a central bank can credibly lower the inflation rate of its currency.

title: Topic 6 - Central Bank Credibility and Inflation Control
text:
Question 1: Central Bank Loss Function and Inflation Bias





Explain why, if the public expect the central bank to set inflation at the equilibrium level \(\pi = \frac{bκλ}{a}\), the central bank will set this inflation rate, rather than \(\pi = 0\), even if it has no intention to create a “surprise” inflation.

title: Topic 6 - Indicative Answers
text:
Tip





The Central Bank’s Loss Function
The central bank has a loss function that reflects its preferences over inflation and output:
\[L = \frac{a}{2}\pi^2 + \frac{b}{2}(Y - Y^T)^2\]
where: - \(\pi\) is inflation - \(Y\) is national income - \(Y^T\) is the CB’s desired level of national income - \(a, b\) reflect the CB’s aversion to inflation and output shortfalls, respectively - \(Y^* = Y^T + \lambda\) where \(Y^*\) is the natural level of output - \(\lambda > 0\) reflects the CB’s preference for income to exceed its natural level (output bias)
Scenario: Public Expects \(\pi = \frac{bκλ}{a}\)
If the CB accommodates this expectation, then from the Lucas AS equation: \[Y = Y^* \text{ (no surprise inflation, so } Y - Y^* = 0\text{)}\]
The loss from the real side: \(\frac{b\lambda^2}{2}\) (output is \(\lambda\) below desired level)
The loss from the inflation side: \(\frac{a}{2}\left(\frac{bκλ}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{bκ^2λ^2}{2a}\)
Total loss under accommodation: \[L = \frac{bλ^2}{2}\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]\]
Alternative: Setting \(\pi = 0\) (Surprise Deflation)
If the CB sets \(\pi = 0\) despite the public expecting \(\pi = \frac{bκλ}{a}\):
From the Lucas AS equation, the price surprise causes output to deviate from potential: \[Y - Y^* = -κ\frac{bκλ}{a}\]
Since \(Y^T = Y^* - \lambda\), the output gap becomes: \[Y - Y^T = -κ\frac{bκλ}{a} + \lambda = -κ\frac{bκ^2λ}{a} + \lambda = λ\left[-\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]\]
The loss from the real side is now much larger: \[L_{\text{real}} = \frac{b}{2}\left[κ\frac{bκλ}{a} + λ\right]^2 = \frac{bλ^2}{2}\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2\]
The inflation loss is zero: \(L_{\text{inflation}} = 0\)
Total loss under surprise deflation: \[L = \frac{bλ^2}{2}\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2\]
Why Accommodation is Preferred
Since \(\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2 > \left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]\), the loss from implementing zero inflation exceeds the loss from accommodating expected inflation.
Key Insight: The Inflation Bias Paradox
Even though the CB has no intention to surprise the public with inflation, it chooses to allow inflation at the expected level because:

The CB has an output target (\(Y^T\)) above the natural rate of output
The public, knowing this, expects accommodating inflation
Disappointing these expectations causes a severe recession that exceeds the inflation costs
The CB prefers accepting expected inflation over the real losses from surprising the public with deflation

This is the essence of time-inconsistency and the inflation bias problem: the CB’s ex-post incentive to accommodate expected inflation conflicts with its ex-ante desire to commit to low inflation. This creates a credibility problem that generates inflation bias in equilibrium.













Tip





The High-Inflation Country Problem
Countries with persistently high inflation often have central banks pursuing excessive monetary growth to achieve real sector objectives. This causes balance-of-payments deficits against low-inflation countries. Under floating exchange rates, the high-inflation currency depreciates, reflecting the difference in inflation rates.
The Fixed Exchange Rate Solution
One approach for a high-inflation country to reduce inflation is to unilaterally fix its exchange rate against a low-inflation anchor currency. Once fixed, the money supply can no longer be set independently—the country must match the anchor currency’s inflation rate to maintain the peg. By surrendering monetary autonomy, the CB signals commitment to low inflation.
Problems with Fixed Exchange Rates:
(i) Weak Commitment Signal
Fixing the exchange rate is not the most obvious or direct way to signal commitment to low inflation. Other mechanisms might more clearly demonstrate policy resolve without restricting policy flexibility.
(ii) Recurring Balance-of-Payments Deficits
If the fixed rate is set too low (too many units of local currency per anchor currency unit), the economy experiences recurring trade deficits. These deficits steadily deplete the central bank’s foreign exchange reserves, which cannot be replenished if monetary growth is constrained. Eventually, reserve depletion forces either devaluation or regime abandonment.
(iii) Loss of Monetary Autonomy During Shocks
When recessionary technology or demand shocks hit the economy, the CB may want to expand the money supply to stabilise domestic output. But the fixed rate peg prevents this, forcing the economy to bear the full burden of adjustment through price and wage deflation—a costly process.
(iv) Speculative Attacks
If markets suspect the peg is unsustainable (due to depleting reserves or political pressure to abandon it), they may engage in speculative attacks—selling the currency en masse to force devaluation. These attacks can be self-fulfilling, destroying reserves and forcing the very devaluation speculators expected.
Alternative Credibility Mechanisms:
(i) Adopting Policy Rules Rather Than Discretion
Instead of relying on discretionary decisions, the CB can commit to a transparent rule—e.g., “the money supply grows at 2% annually” or “inflation must stay within a 1-3% band.” Rules constrain the CB’s ability to pursue short-term output objectives and make policy predictable. However, rules limit flexibility during genuine emergencies.
(ii) Appointing a Conservative, Inflation-Hawk Central Banker
Credibility can be strengthened by appointing a CB governor known to be strongly committed to price stability and skeptical of inflation. If the CB leader has a public reputation as an inflation-hawk, markets and the public expect low inflation regardless of political pressure. Examples include Paul Volcker (US Fed) or the Bundesbank leadership.
(iii) Performance-Based Compensation and Incentive Schemes
Add personal financial rewards and penalties to CB officials’ compensation based on inflation outcomes. For example, senior CB managers receive bonuses if inflation stays below target but face penalties if it exceeds target. This aligns personal incentives with low-inflation objectives, counteracting bureaucratic or political biases toward expansionary policy. It makes the commitment credible because officials’ own financial interests depend on delivering low inflation.
Comparative Effectiveness
These mechanisms address the time-inconsistency problem differently: - Rules eliminate discretion ex-post - Conservative leadership creates strong ex-ante reputation and expectations of resistance to inflation - Performance incentives align individual incentives with institutional objectives, making officials directly accountable
The most credible approach typically combines multiple mechanisms: clear rules, conservative leadership, transparency, and performance accountability.

Alternative: Setting \(\pi = 0\) (Surprise Deflation)
If the CB sets \(\pi = 0\) despite the public expecting \(\pi = \frac{bκλ}{a}\):
From the Lucas AS equation, the price surprise causes output to deviate from potential: \[Y - Y^* = -κ\frac{bκλ}{a}\]
Since \(Y^T = Y^* - \lambda\), the output gap becomes: \[Y - Y^T = -κ\frac{bκλ}{a} + \lambda = -κ\frac{bκ^2λ}{a} + \lambda = λ\left[-\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]\]
The loss from the real side is now much larger: \[L_{\text{real}} = \frac{b}{2}\left[κ\frac{bκλ}{a} + λ\right]^2 = \frac{bλ^2}{2}\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2\]
The inflation loss is zero: \(L_{\text{inflation}} = 0\)
Total loss under surprise deflation: \[L = \frac{bλ^2}{2}\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2\]
Why Accommodation is Preferred
Since \(\left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]^2 > \left[\frac{bκ^2}{a} + 1\right]\), the loss from implementing zero inflation exceeds the loss from accommodating expected inflation.
Key Insight: The Inflation Bias Paradox
Even though the CB has no intention to surprise the public with inflation, it chooses to allow inflation at the expected level because:

The CB has an output target (\(Y^T\)) above the natural rate of output
The public, knowing this, expects accommodating inflation
Disappointing these expectations causes a severe recession that exceeds the inflation costs
The CB prefers accepting expected inflation over the real losses from surprising the public with deflation

This is the essence of time-inconsistency and the inflation bias problem: the CB’s ex-post incentive to accommodate expected inflation conflicts with its ex-ante desire to commit to low inflation. This creates a credibility problem that generates inflation bias in equilibrium.

title: Topic 6 - Indicative Answers
text:
Tip





The High-Inflation Country Problem
Countries with persistently high inflation often have central banks pursuing excessive monetary growth to achieve real sector objectives. This causes balance-of-payments deficits against low-inflation countries. Under floating exchange rates, the high-inflation currency depreciates, reflecting the difference in inflation rates.
The Fixed Exchange Rate Solution
One approach for a high-inflation country to reduce inflation is to unilaterally fix its exchange rate against a low-inflation anchor currency. Once fixed, the money supply can no longer be set independently—the country must match the anchor currency’s inflation rate to maintain the peg. By surrendering monetary autonomy, the CB signals commitment to low inflation.
Problems with Fixed Exchange Rates:
(i) Weak Commitment Signal
Fixing the exchange rate is not the most obvious or direct way to signal commitment to low inflation. Other mechanisms might more clearly demonstrate policy resolve without restricting policy flexibility.
(ii) Recurring Balance-of-Payments Deficits
If the fixed rate is set too low (too many units of local currency per anchor currency unit), the economy experiences recurring trade deficits. These deficits steadily deplete the central bank’s foreign exchange reserves, which cannot be replenished if monetary growth is constrained. Eventually, reserve depletion forces either devaluation or regime abandonment.
(iii) Loss of Monetary Autonomy During Shocks
When recessionary technology or demand shocks hit the economy, the CB may want to expand the money supply to stabilise domestic output. But the fixed rate peg prevents this, forcing the economy to bear the full burden of adjustment through price and wage deflation—a costly process.
(iv) Speculative Attacks
If markets suspect the peg is unsustainable (due to depleting reserves or political pressure to abandon it), they may engage in speculative attacks—selling the currency en masse to force devaluation. These attacks can be self-fulfilling, destroying reserves and forcing the very devaluation speculators expected.
Alternative Credibility Mechanisms:
(i) Adopting Policy Rules Rather Than Discretion
Instead of relying on discretionary decisions, the CB can commit to a transparent rule—e.g., “the money supply grows at 2% annually” or “inflation must stay within a 1-3% band.” Rules constrain the CB’s ability to pursue short-term output objectives and make policy predictable. However, rules limit flexibility during genuine emergencies.
(ii) Appointing a Conservative, Inflation-Hawk Central Banker
Credibility can be strengthened by appointing a CB governor known to be strongly committed to price stability and skeptical of inflation. If the CB leader has a public reputation as an inflation-hawk, markets and the public expect low inflation regardless of political pressure. Examples include Paul Volcker (US Fed) or the Bundesbank leadership.
(iii) Performance-Based Compensation and Incentive Schemes
Add personal financial rewards and penalties to CB officials’ compensation based on inflation outcomes. For example, senior CB managers receive bonuses if inflation stays below target but face penalties if it exceeds target. This aligns personal incentives with low-inflation objectives, counteracting bureaucratic or political biases toward expansionary policy. It makes the commitment credible because officials’ own financial interests depend on delivering low inflation.
Comparative Effectiveness
These mechanisms address the time-inconsistency problem differently: - Rules eliminate discretion ex-post - Conservative leadership creates strong ex-ante reputation and expectations of resistance to inflation - Performance incentives align individual incentives with institutional objectives, making officials directly accountable
The most credible approach typically combines multiple mechanisms: clear rules, conservative leadership, transparency, and performance accountability.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
The New Classical approach extends monetarist skepticism about policy fine-tuning by sharpening the mechanism through which policy affects real outcomes. The key shift is from short-run money illusion under adaptive expectations (Friedman’s framework) to model-consistent forecasting under rational expectations, which removes systematic policy surprises and eliminates systematic real effects of monetary policy.




Adaptive expectations operate as a trial-and-error forecasting rule where agents update forecasts using past observed outcomes:
Price expectations: \(E_{t-1}P_t = f(P_{t-1}, P_{t-2}, ...)\)
A common error-correction form is: \[\pi_t^e = \pi_{t-1}^e + \lambda(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-1}^e), \quad 0 < \lambda \le 1.\]
Adaptive expectations permit systematic forecast errors during regime changes, creating temporary money illusion and thus temporary real effects.



Rational expectations are defined by three criteria: (i) forecasts use the true economic model (agents know the economy’s structure), (ii) forecasts condition on all available information, and (iii) forecast errors are purely random—systematic errors are eliminated.
In classical formulation: expectations are “the same as the predictions of the relevant economic theory,” and the economy does not waste information.
Model-consistent forecasting: \[E_{t-1}P_t = E(P_t \mid I_{t-1}),\] where \(I_{t-1}\) is the information set at time \(t-1\).
If workers have access to unbiased forecasts, predictable policy loses its ability to manipulate perceived real wages and thus loses its ability to shift real output, even in the short run.

title: The New Classical Approach
section: 2.1 Lucas aggregate supply and aggregate demand
text:
2.1 Lucas aggregate supply and aggregate demand
Figure 1. Lucas aggregate supply: output deviates from potential only when P differs from expected price. If expectations are correct, output remains at potential.








Figure 1: Lucas Aggregate Supply: \(Y_t - Y^* = \kappa(P_t - E_{t-1}P_t)\)





The New Classical model consists of two equations: Lucas supply (LAS) and aggregate demand (AD).
Lucas aggregate supply (LAS): Output deviates from potential only when the price level differs from expectations: \[Y_t^s - Y^* = \kappa(P_t - E_{t-1}P_t).\]
Lucas (1972) derives this in a market-clearing framework with optimizing agents.
Interpretation: - If \(P_t > E_{t-1}P_t\): firms perceive relative-price gains, supply rises (\(Y_t^s > Y^*\)) - If \(P_t = E_{t-1}P_t\): output at potential (\(Y_t^s = Y^*\)) - If \(P_t < E_{t-1}P_t\): output below potential (\(Y_t^s < Y^*\))
The parameter \(\kappa\) measures supply responsiveness: \(\partial Y_t / \partial(P_t - E_{t-1}P_t) = \kappa\).
Aggregate demand (AD): In log form: \[Y_t^d = \gamma + M_t - P_t,\] where \(M_t\) is nominal money and \(\gamma\) captures exogenous demand shifts.
Agents know structural parameters \(\gamma\), \(\kappa\), and natural output \(Y^*\).

title: The New Classical Approach
section: 2.2 Solving the model: the role of \(\kappa\)
text:
2.2 Solving the model: the role of \(\kappa\)
Equilibrium: \(Y_t^s = Y_t^d = Y_t\). Combining LAS and AD:

Under rational expectations: \[E_{t-1}Y_t = Y^*.\]
Output deviations depend only on monetary surprises: \[Y_t - Y^* = \frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}(M_t - E_{t-1}M_t).\]
Price surprises scale with monetary surprises: \[P_t - E_{t-1}P_t = \frac{1}{1+\kappa}(M_t - E_{t-1}M_t).\]

Interpretation: larger \(\kappa\) means output responds more, prices respond less; smaller \(\kappa\) reverses this. The Lucas supply slope (P on vertical axis, Y horizontal) is proportional to \(1/\kappa\).
When policy is volatile, agents discount price movements as noise (“boy who cried wolf”), lowering effective \(\kappa\) and steepening LAS.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
3.1 The monetary policy ineffectiveness proposition
With rational expectations and market clearing, systematic and predictable monetary policy has no real effect, even short-run. Predictable policy is incorporated into expectations, shifting prices, not real outcomes.
Formally, if \(M_t = E_{t-1}M_t\) (policy is forecastable): \[Y_t - Y^* = 0.\]

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
3.2 Systematic rules versus random disturbances
Figure 2. Predictable versus unpredictable monetary policy. A predictable rise in money shifts AD and LAS upward (via expectations); equilibrium stays at \(Y^*\). An unpredictable rise shifts AD without shifting LAS initially; equilibrium moves along LAS with \(Y\) above \(Y^*\).








Figure 2: Policy predictability determines whether output effects are temporary.





Sharp distinction: (i) predictable rule-like policy vs. (ii) random disturbances.
Money supply process: \[M_t = (1 + g_M)M_{t-1} + u_t,\] where \(u_t\) is white noise (\(E_{t-1}u_t = 0\)).
Then: \(E_{t-1}M_t = (1 + g_M)M_{t-1}\), so \(M_t - E_{t-1}M_t = u_t\).
Output deviations: \[Y_t - Y^* = \frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}u_t.\]
Only randomness affects output. Predictable money growth affects the price level, not real activity.

title: The New Classical Approach
section: 3.3 Why deliberate unpredictability is not recommended
text:
3.3 Why deliberate unpredictability is not recommended
Figure 3. Policy volatility reduces supply responsiveness via information effects. Greater policy volatility lowers the informational content of observed price movements. Agents cannot distinguish relative-price signals from aggregate noise, reducing supply response (lower \(\kappa\)) and steepening LAS.








Figure 3: Higher policy volatility steepens Lucas supply through information effects.





The model should not justify randomness. Two reasons:

Random policies produce recessions and booms equally (negative \(u_t\) as likely as positive).
High volatility changes behaviour: agents discount price signals, steepening LAS (lower effective \(\kappa\), higher price response).

This logic explains modern central-bank transparency: policy is more effective when expectations are anchored and communication reduces unnecessary uncertainty.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
4.1 Asymmetric information and real shocks
If productivity shocks drive cycles and the central bank forecasts a negative shock before the private sector, it can expand policy in advance to stabilise output (at higher prices).
This fits the New Classical framework because the CB has an informational advantage, creating a price surprise from the public’s perspective.
Compatible with real-business-cycle reasoning: technology/productivity shocks drive cycles.

title: The New Classical Approach
section: 4.2 Long-term nominal wage contracts and stabilisation
text:
4.2 Long-term nominal wage contracts and stabilisation
In many economies, nominal wages are fixed by multi-year contracts. Even if demand shocks are anticipated, monetary policy can offset them because some nominal wages cannot adjust immediately—rigidity creates stabilisation scope.
This aligns with Fischer (1977): under wage rigidity, monetary rules interact with shock propagation even under rational expectations.
Under symmetric information (no CB informational advantage), stabilisation works best for demand shocks; supply-side stabilisation requires informational asymmetry.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
4.3 Lucas critique and credibility
The Lucas critique: policy-effect estimates from historical relationships are unreliable if decision rules shift with the regime. This motivates structural, microfounded models.
If agents form expectations rationally, commitment and credibility shape outcomes through expectations. Rules, strategy statements, and transparent communication are policy tools.
Time-inconsistency literature: policy is strategic interaction with rational agents. Discretionary optimisation can backfire because promises today are not optimal tomorrow (after expectations set). Central to rules-versus-discretion analysis.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
5.1 Measuring policy surprises
New Classical model disturbance: \(M_t - E_{t-1}M_t\). Modern empirical work isolates surprise components using high-frequency financial data.
Recent IMF working paper: dataset of monetary policy shocks for 21 advanced and 8 emerging economies (2000–2022), using daily changes in interest rate swap rates around central bank announcements to identify unexpected policy shocks to the rate path. Maps directly to model: unexpected shocks are the empirical analogue of \(u_t\).

title: The New Classical Approach
section: 5.2 Credibility and anchored expectations in practice
text:
5.2 Credibility and anchored expectations in practice
New Classical analysis makes credibility central. Modern CBs frame policy as expectations management.
Federal Reserve: publishing its “Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy” helps the public understand the framework—matters for transparency, accountability, and effectiveness.
ECB (2021 strategy): symmetric 2% medium-term inflation aim; notes that effective lower bound can require “especially forceful or persistent” measures, including transitory inflation above target.
IMF research: better-anchored expectations → less persistent inflation responses to shocks, reinforcing New Classical emphasis on credibility and expectations formation.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
5.3 Policy regime episodes
Bank of Japan: reference timeline documents unconventional regimes from late 1990s onward (ZIRP 1999, QE from 2001). Explicitly lists “policy duration effect (forward guidance)” as part of ZIRP—an expectations-management concept compatible with New Classical theory.
Japan’s 2024 framework change: QQE with yield curve control and negative rates judged to have “fulfilled their roles,” shifting back to short-rate guidance—regime transition where expectations and credibility matter.
ECB (June 2014): introducing negative deposit facility rate (–0.10% effective June 11, 2014) illustrates how rules change when constraints bind and why expectation formation is central to transmission.
COVID-19 emergency actions: central banks reacted with large-scale measures for market functioning and macro stabilisation, showing regime and expectations logic when short rates are constrained.

title: The New Classical Approach
text:
5.4 Comparative framework: mechanisms and applications








Mechanism
Prediction
Modern illustration




Systematic, predictable policy
If anticipated, shifts \(E_{t-1}P_t\) one-for-one; \(Y_t \approx Y^*\)
Fed and ECB strategy statements anchor expectations through transparency.


Unanticipated shocks
Only surprise component drives \(P_t - E_{t-1}P_t\), hence \(Y_t - Y^*\)
IMF high-frequency dataset (2000–2022) identifies unexpected policy shocks at announcements.


Policy volatility
Agents discount price signals; LAS steepens (lower effective \(\kappa\))
CBs prefer predictable reaction functions over crisis-era surprise moves.


Wage contracts
Nominal rigidity reopens stabilisation, even under rational expectations
BoE COVID interventions supported market functioning and prevented tightening.


Informational advantage
CB with better real-shock information can offset systematically
BoJ forward guidance and regime design link to RBC-style productivity shocks.

title: Topic 5 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
How to use this quiz



This quiz is designed as a formative self-assessment tool, not as a test.
Its purpose is to help you: - check your understanding of the key concepts from Topic 5, - identify which types of thinking you find more difficult, and - guide your revision before the tutorial and future assessments.


Each question belongs to one of four categories:

Subject Knowledge (SK): definitions, concepts, and facts.

Analysis (AN): understanding relationships and economic mechanisms.

Problem Solving (PS): applying concepts to new situations.

Mathematical Thinking (MT): working with equations and quantitative relationships.

Your score will be broken down by category so you can see where you are strong and where you need more practice.




You may use your notes and the lecture materials.
Take your time — the goal is understanding, not speed.
Use the Hints if you get stuck.
You may refresh and retry the quiz as many times as you like.





A low score is not a problem — it tells you what to focus on.
If you score low in:

SK: revise definitions and core concepts.
AN: revisit the logic of the models and examples.
PS: practise applying concepts to new cases.
MT: practise the mathematical calculations and equations.





The leaderboard is optional and anonymous. It exists only to make practice more engaging.
It has no effect on your grade and is not used for evaluation.
The only purpose of this quiz is to support your learning.

title: Topic 4 - Friedman’s Monetarism
text:
Question 1: Monetarist Model of the Labour Market





Consider the following monetarist model of the macroeconomy. The labour market is characterised by
\[N^S = 100\theta\] \[N^D = \frac{6400}{\theta^2}\]
where \(N^S\) is the supply of labour, \(N^D\) is labour demand and \(\theta\) is shorthand for the real wage (i.e. \(W/P\): \(W\) is the nominal wage and \(P\) the price level).
The production function is \[Y = 160\sqrt{N}\]
where \(N\) is the labour employed when the labour market is in equilibrium.
The demand side of the economy is characterised by the Quantity Theory of Money: \[M = 2PY\]
where \(M\) is the money supply and the proportionality constant is \(k = 2\).

Verify that the above equation describing labour demand is consistent with the production function (i.e. labour demand is at the point where the marginal product of labour is equal to the real wage).
Solve for the equilibrium values of \(\theta\) and \(N\) and plugging the latter into the production function, solve for \(Y\).
Suppose that the initial money supply, \(M_0 = 32000\). Solve for \(P_0\) and \(W_0\).

text:
Question 1: Monetarist Model of the Labour Market





Consider the following monetarist model of the macroeconomy. The labour market is characterised by
\[N^S = 100\theta\] \[N^D = \frac{6400}{\theta^2}\]
where \(N^S\) is the supply of labour, \(N^D\) is labour demand and \(\theta\) is shorthand for the real wage (i.e. \(W/P\): \(W\) is the nominal wage and \(P\) the price level).
The production function is \[Y = 160\sqrt{N}\]
where \(N\) is the labour employed when the labour market is in equilibrium.
The demand side of the economy is characterised by the Quantity Theory of Money: \[M = 2PY\]
where \(M\) is the money supply and the proportionality constant is \(k = 2\).

Verify that the above equation describing labour demand is consistent with the production function (i.e. labour demand is at the point where the marginal product of labour is equal to the real wage).
Solve for the equilibrium values of \(\theta\) and \(N\) and plugging the latter into the production function, solve for \(Y\).
Suppose that the initial money supply, \(M_0 = 32000\). Solve for \(P_0\) and \(W_0\).

title: Topic 4 - Indicative Answers
text:
Part (a)





From the production function, the marginal product of labour is: \[\frac{\partial Y}{\partial N} = \frac{160}{2\sqrt{N}} = \frac{80}{\sqrt{N}}\]
When firms maximise profit, they hire labour until \(MPN = \theta\). Therefore: \[\theta = \frac{80}{\sqrt{N}}\] \[\sqrt{N} = \frac{80}{\theta}\] \[N = \frac{6400}{\theta^2}\]
This matches the given labour demand equation, confirming consistency. ✓


Setting \(N^S = N^D\): \[100\theta = \frac{6400}{\theta^2}\] \[100\theta^3 = 6400\] \[\theta^3 = 64\] \[\theta = 4\]
Therefore: \(N = 100 \times 4 = 400\)
Substituting into the production function: \[Y = 160\sqrt{400} = 160 \times 20 = 3200\]



From the QTM: \(P = \frac{M}{kY}\)
With \(M_0 = 32000\) and \(k = 2\): \[P_0 = \frac{32000}{2 \times 3200} = \frac{32000}{6400} = 5\]
The money wage is: \[W_0 = \theta \times P_0 = 4 \times 5 = 20\]



With \(M_1 = 48000\): \[P_1 = \frac{48000}{2 \times 3200} = \frac{48000}{6400} = 7.5\]
In long-run equilibrium, the labour market remains at its natural level regardless of money supply changes. Therefore: \[\theta = 4, \quad N = 400, \quad Y = 3200 \text{ (unchanged)}\] \[W_1 = 4 \times 7.5 = 30\]



Yes, the model exhibits dichotomy and neutrality of money. Real variables (\(\theta\), \(N\), \(Y\)) are determined solely by production technology and labour supply preferences, independent of the money supply. A 50% increase in \(M\) (from 32000 to 48000) causes exactly proportional increases in nominal variables (prices and wages double from \(5 \to 7.5\), \(20 \to 30\)) but leaves all real variables unchanged. This demonstrates classical neutrality: in the long run, money is a veil over the real economy.














Part (a)





With workers using \(P_0 = 5\) as the reference price: \[N^S = 100\frac{W'}{5} = 20W'\]
Setting \(N^S = N^D\): \[20W' = \frac{6400}{(\theta')^2} = \frac{6400(P')^2}{(W')^2}\] \[(W')^3 = \frac{6400(P')^2}{20} = 320(P')^2\] \[P' = \frac{\sqrt{(W')^3}}{\sqrt{320}} = \frac{(W')^{3/2}}{\sqrt{320}} = \frac{\sqrt{80}(W')^{3/2}}{160}\]


From the labour supply: \(N' = 20W'\)
Plugging into production function: \[Y' = 160\sqrt{20W'}\]
From the QTM with \(M_1 = 48000\): \[P' = \frac{M_1}{kY'} = \frac{48000}{2 \times 160\sqrt{20W'}} = \frac{150}{\sqrt{20W'}}\]



Equating the two expressions for \(P'\): \[\frac{\sqrt{80}(W')^{3/2}}{160} = \frac{150}{\sqrt{20W'}}\]
Solving: \[(W')^2 = \frac{150^2 \times 160^2}{80 \times 20} = 600\] \[W' \approx 24.49\]
Therefore: \[N' = 20 \times 24.49 = 489.8\] \[Y' = 160\sqrt{489.8} \approx 3545.7\] \[P' = \frac{48000}{2 \times 3545.7} \approx 6.76\] \[\theta' = \frac{W'}{P'} = \frac{24.49}{6.76} \approx 3.62\]
Note that \(\theta' = 3.62 < 4 = \theta_0\), but \(W' = 24.49 > 20 = W_0\). Workers perceive a wage rise even though the real wage has fallen!



Verifying labour market equilibrium at \(\theta' = 3.62\): \[N^S = 20 \times 24.49 = 489.8\] \[N^D = \frac{6400}{(3.62)^2} \approx 488.5 \approx N^S\] ✓
Labour market clears in the short run.



Friedman’s key insight: Money illusion creates short-run non-neutrality. Workers observe \(W' > W_0\) and perceive a real wage increase even though \(\theta' < \theta_0\). This illusion causes labour supply to expand far beyond its natural level, pulling down the real wage and increasing both employment and output above their long-run levels.
Short run: Monetary expansion stimulates employment (\(N' = 489.8 > 400\)) and output (\(Y' = 3545.7 > 3200\)) because workers are fooled about inflation.
Long run: When workers eventually recognise that \(P'\) has risen more than \(W'\), they realise their real wage has fallen. Labour supply contracts back to its natural level, \(N\) returns to 400, \(Y\) reverts to 3200, and \(\theta\) returns to 4.
This supports Friedman’s argument that monetary policy has temporary real effects in the short run but is neutral in the long run—the lag between actual and perceived inflation is crucial to short-run monetary non-neutrality. The Phillips curve is downward-sloping in the short run (trade-off between inflation and unemployment) but vertical in the long run (no permanent trade-off).














Part (a)





From the dynamic QTM: \[\pi = g_M - g_Y = 3\% - 1\% = 2\%\]
From the Fisher equation: \[i = r + \pi = 2\% + 2\% = 4\%\]


When \(g_M\) accelerates from \(3\%\) to \(6\%\):
Short Run:

(i) Growth rate of output temporarily rises above \(1\%\) (to ~\(1.5\%\)). The increase in money growth stimulates employment and output via money illusion. Workers see nominal wages rising faster than expected and supply more labour, pushing output above trend.
(ii) Rate of inflation rises but lags the increase in money growth (to ~\(3-4\%\), less than the full \(5\%\)). Initially, prices adjust slowly while the monetary expansion feeds into employment growth. The inflation gap (\(g_M - \pi > 0\)) creates the real stimulus.
(iii) Nominal interest rate initially falls below \(4\%\) (to ~\(3\%\)). Real rates are pushed down as inflation expectations lag, and the output boom creates downward pressure on interest rates.
(iv) Real interest rate falls temporarily below \(2\%\) into negative territory. The excess money supply and output expansion compress real returns.

Long Run:

(i) Growth rate of output returns to \(1\%\). Once workers and firms perceive the true inflation, they adjust expectations. Labour supply reverts to its natural level, and output growth returns to its trend determined by labour force growth and technology.
(ii) Rate of inflation settles at \(\pi = g_M - g_Y = 6\% - 1\% = 5\%\). The full monetary impulse translates to inflation once expectations fully adjust.
(iii) Nominal interest rate rises to \(i = r + \pi = 2\% + 5\% = 7\%\). Higher inflation raises nominal rates accordingly.
(iv) Real interest rate returns to \(2\%\). The real rate is determined by real fundamentals (time preferences, productivity) independent of monetary growth. Monetary changes affect only nominal magnitudes in the long run.

Short Run:

(i) Growth rate of output temporarily rises above \(1\%\) (to ~\(1.5\%\)). The increase in money growth stimulates employment and output via money illusion. Workers see nominal wages rising faster than expected and supply more labour, pushing output above trend.
(ii) Rate of inflation rises but lags the increase in money growth (to ~\(3-4\%\), less than the full \(5\%\)). Initially, prices adjust slowly while the monetary expansion feeds into employment growth. The inflation gap (\(g_M - \pi > 0\)) creates the real stimulus.
(iii) Nominal interest rate initially falls below \(4\%\) (to ~\(3\%\)). Real rates are pushed down as inflation expectations lag, and the output boom creates downward pressure on interest rates.
(iv) Real interest rate falls temporarily below \(2\%\) into negative territory. The excess money supply and output expansion compress real returns.

Long Run:

(i) Growth rate of output returns to \(1\%\). Once workers and firms perceive the true inflation, they adjust expectations. Labour supply reverts to its natural level, and output growth returns to its trend determined by labour force growth and technology.
(ii) Rate of inflation settles at \(\pi = g_M - g_Y = 6\% - 1\% = 5\%\). The full monetary impulse translates to inflation once expectations fully adjust.
(iii) Nominal interest rate rises to \(i = r + \pi = 2\% + 5\% = 7\%\). Higher inflation raises nominal rates accordingly.
(iv) Real interest rate returns to \(2\%\). The real rate is determined by real fundamentals (time preferences, productivity) independent of monetary growth. Monetary changes affect only nominal magnitudes in the long run.

Diagrams:
